profile.name: Waacking
profile.tagline: Explosive overhead arm rolls, cinematic poses, and theatrical disco expression.
profile.insight: Born in 1970s Los Angeles gay clubs under the slur 'punking', dancers reclaimed the movement into waacking by channelling the fierce glamour of classic Hollywood screen icons.
profile.profile: Waacking is an African American and Latino street dance style created during the 1970s disco era within the LGBTQ+ club scene of Los Angeles. Originating from punking, the dance isolates explosive, rotational arm movements over the head alongside dramatic cinematic posing and emotional storytelling. Dancers originally took stylistic cues from stars such as Lauren Bacall, Marlene Dietrich, and James Dean while moving to accelerated underground disco and funk. Nearly extinguished by the AIDS crisis in the 1980s and 1990s, waacking was revitalised in the 2000s and has expanded onto world television stages, music videos, and Olympic ice.
profile.profile_long:
Waacking emerged during the early 1970s within the underground LGBTQ+ club scene of Los Angeles, developed primarily by African American and Latino dancers. In its inception, the movement was known as punking, repurposing a contemporary derogatory slur directed at gay men. Within this culture, men performed heightened, sensual, and feminine movement expressions, channelling theatrical storytelling to imported, accelerated disco and funk tracks. The specific explosive gesture of striking the arms overhead in time with the music was called a 'whack'. As the dance migrated outward into broader venues and television stages such as Soul Train, heterosexual club-goers and performers adopted the form under the name 'whacking' to shed homophobic connotations. Dancer and singer-songwriter Jeffrey Daniel added the final letter 'g', establishing the spelling 'waacking' that was widely embraced.

The aesthetic core of waacking is defined by rapid, rotational arm trajectories, sharp overhead wraps, and sudden frozen poses executed with vivid emotional expression. Drawing inspiration from Hollywood cinema of the 1920s and Golden Age stars like Lauren Bacall, Marlene Dietrich, Bette Davis, and James Dean, dancers translated cinematic diva attitudes, facial drama, and glamorous costuming onto the nightclub floor. While waacking shares visual similarities with locking—another Los Angeles street style developed during the exact same period—the two styles diverged along musical and social lines: locking grew out of the broader funk scene, whereas waacking was cultivated in queer spaces on an unrelenting foundation of high-tempo disco.

The dance faced a devastating rupture during the 1980s and 1990s when the HIV/AIDS epidemic claimed the lives of most of its foundational generation, causing the tradition to almost completely disappear from public view. Survival rested on television archives, memory, and a small circle of surviving pioneers such as Soul Train veteran Tyrone Proctor. In 2003, dancer Brian Green, known as 'Footwork', identified the urgent breakdown in cultural transmission and began teaching waacking internationally, sparking a worldwide revival. Dancers embraced the form across battle circuits, theatrical stages, and commercial choreography. In 2011, Kumari Suraj choreographed a waacking routine on So You Think You Can Dance, introducing the style to modern television audiences, while Josépha Madoki performed waacking in Beyoncé and Jay-Z's 2018 music video for 'Apeshit'. At the 2022 Winter Olympics, ice dancers Gabriella Papadakis and Guillaume Cizeron incorporated waacking into their world record-breaking rhythm dance, demonstrating the global reach of a style forged on underground dance floors.

sections.origins_and_history: Waacking originated in Los Angeles during the early 1970s inside LGBTQ+ nightclubs, created primarily by African American and Latino dancers. It began as punking, a name derived from a derogatory slur aimed at gay men, which performers inverted into an expressive, narrative dance style. Dancers moved to underground and imported disco music that DJs sped up to produce an intense, energetic atmosphere. The specific technique of driving the arms over the head in rhythm became known as 'whack'. Heterosexual dancers who encountered the style renamed it whacking to distance themselves from anti-gay terminology, after which gay culture reclaimed and reshaped the term into 'waacking', formalized when Soul Train dancer and singer-songwriter Jeffrey Daniel added the 'g'. During the 1980s and 1990s, the AIDS crisis killed most of the style's iconic pioneers, driving the dance close to extinction until Brian 'Footwork' Green began teaching it in 2003 to ensure its transmission.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The style is executed through rapid, rotational arm sweeps, explosive rhythmic strikes, and theatrical poses coordinated with music. Dancers whip their forearms and wrists around and behind the head and across the shoulder line, isolating sharp gestures while maintaining rhythmic syncopation. A key technical element is posing, in which dancers freeze into glamorous, heightened diva stances inspired by Hollywood movie figures. The dance prioritizes facial expression, sensuality, and dramatic storytelling, allowing the performer to embody distinct attitudes and narrative moods. Footwork in the sources incorporates elements derived from jazz, gymnastics, martial arts, and hip-hop influences, though the central visual hallmark remains overhead arm isolations danced to fast tempos.
sections.music_and_instruments: Waacking was founded on 1970s disco and funk, specifically underground and imported disco records that were often sped up on club turntables to increase dance floor energy. Over subsequent decades, the dance adapted to 1980s post-disco, electro sounds, and modern music varieties, though disco remains its historical and primary sonic foundation. The music is characterized by steady four-on-the-floor percussion, driving basslines, orchestral sweeps, and brass hits that provide sharp rhythmic accents for explosive arm strikes and sudden poses.
sections.costume_and_setting: Originally performed in dimly lit LGBTQ+ nightclubs of 1970s Los Angeles, waacking was framed by social freedom and theatrical display. Dancers drew visual and sartorial inspiration from classic Hollywood screen stars such as Marlene Dietrich, Lauren Bacall, and James Dean, adopting vintage diva attitudes, tailored silhouettes, and stylized garments. In modern practice, waacking appears in international dance battles, television studios, university theatre departments, music videos, and competitive ice rinks, where performers continue to wear expressive, high-fashion, and dramatic attire.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: In its original gay club context, punking and waacking served as an outlet of creative liberation, sensual expression, and self-definition for marginalized queer, Black, and Latino dancers facing social hostility. The dance provided a theatrical space to emulate glamorous Hollywood divas and enact personal stories through heightened physicality. Today, waacking is performed at competitive street dance battles, theatre showcases, university dance curricula, pop concerts, and global sports ceremonies, retaining its ethos of unapologetic self-expression and dramatic presence.
sections.notable_figures: Key historical and contemporary figures include Jeffrey Daniel, who added the 'g' to the name; Tyrone Proctor (1953–2020), a pioneering Los Angeles creator and Soul Train dancer; Brian 'Footwork' Green, who initiated the 2003 global revival through workshops; Kumari Suraj, who choreographed a milestone 2011 routine on So You Think You Can Dance; and French waacker Josépha Madoki, who danced in the 2018 'Apeshit' music video by Beyoncé and Jay-Z. Other notable practitioners named in sources include Bruno Marignan, Sandrine Sainte Croix, Lil Kiss, Princess Lockeroo, Mariana Benenge, Mounia Nassangar, Habibitch, Boubou, choreographer Axelle Munezero, and Olympic champions Gabriella Papadakis and Guillaume Cizeron.
sections.regional_variants: Waacking originated in Los Angeles, California, developing alongside New York City's parallel ballroom voguing culture on the East Coast of the United States. While early waacking was centered in southern California venues and national broadcast sets like Soul Train, contemporary regional hubs have expanded globally. France has emerged as a significant center through artists like Josépha Madoki, Princess Lockeroo, and choreographers who adapted the style for theater and international competition.
sections.lineage: Waacking evolved directly out of punking in 1970s Los Angeles gay clubs, absorbing stylistic and physical principles from jazz dance, gymnastics, martial arts, and Hollywood screen performance. It developed alongside locking within the Los Angeles street dance ecosystem and runs historically parallel to East Coast voguing. In modern lineages, waacking has exchanged vocabulary with hip-hop dance and entered university dance departments as well as commercial performance repertoires.

basic_steps: Arm Whack: rhythmic strike bringing forearm and hand sharply over the head
Rotational Overhead Sweep: continuous circular winding of arms around the crown and neck
Hollywood Diva Pose: sudden frozen stylized silhouette imitating classic film screen actors
Rhythmic Extension: extending arms explosively outward to music accents before returning to overhead rotation
teaching.rhythm: Fast 4/4 disco and post-disco pulse, emphasizing sharp syncopated hits on downbeats and snare snaps
teaching.formation: Individual freestyle circles, battle cyphers, and staged choreographic group formations
teaching.level_notes: Beginners isolate elbow and wrist rotations slowly before accelerating to 120+ BPM disco speeds and integrating full-body posing

music_profile.rhythm_pattern: Driving four-on-the-floor kick with upbeat open hi-hats and accented syncopated brass and string stabs
music_profile.vocal_style: Dramatic, soulful disco vocals and diva hooks, expressive and high-energy
music_profile.musical_form: Verse-chorus structure with extended instrumental dance breaks and dynamic percussion builds
music_profile.sound_description: High-octane 1970s disco and post-disco characterized by a relentless four-on-the-floor beat, syncopated basslines, and soaring orchestral strings. The music delivers dramatic brass accents and vocal peaks that cue sharp, sudden arm hits and frozen poses.

movement_profile.posture: Upright, proud, theatrical spine with an open chest, projecting diva glamour and continuous eye contact
movement_profile.footwork: Rhythmic stepping and weight shifts supporting torso orientation, influenced by jazz and club social steps
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Rapid rotational arm movements, wrist isolations, and over-the-head whacks coordinated with musical accents
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Sensual, dynamic torso lines with rhythmic rib isolations and fluid hip shifts
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Solo cypher center, moving dynamically within an intimate personal sphere or across a performance stage
movement_profile.partnering: Primarily solo freestyle; in battles, dancers face each other dialogically; staged synchronization in choreographies
movement_profile.tempo_feel: Urgent, driving, and razor-sharp, maintaining fluid arm circles between instantaneous frozen accents

signature_moves.name: The Whack
signature_moves.description: An explosive movement of the forearm and hand driving up and over the head in strict musical rhythm

signature_moves.name: Posing
signature_moves.description: Dramatic, frozen attitudes channeling vintage Hollywood film stars with stylized hand and head placement

signature_moves.name: Rotational Arm Rolls
signature_moves.description: Continuous circular loops of the forearms around the head, shoulders, and chest without breaking tempo

movement_profile.levels_and_jumps: Primarily danced upright, incorporating low floor lunges, drops, and dynamic level changes during dramatic musical breaks
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Do not execute arm rolls without shoulder warming; avoid disconnecting arm movement from musical phrasing or facial expression

episode_brief.title_hook: When a Slur Became a Symphony of Arms
episode_brief.logline: Inside the underground queer clubs of 1970s Los Angeles, persecuted dancers took classic Hollywood glamour, accelerated disco, and explosive overhead arm strikes to invent waacking.
beats: 1970s Los Angeles gay nightlife: dancers create punking to fast underground disco records.
The invention of the 'whack' overhead strike and Jeffrey Daniel adding the 'g' to coin 'waacking'.
Hollywood influence: channeling Bette Davis, Lauren Bacall, and James Dean in dramatic poses.
Soul Train broadcast and the creation of The Outrageous Waacking Dancers.
The devastating loss of original pioneers during the 1980s-1990s AIDS crisis.
Brian Green's 2003 classroom revival and the modern resurgence in Paris, pop culture, and Olympic ice.

lesson_ladder.goal: Master the basic arm roll and overhead whack on half-time counts
drills: Single-arm wrist circle over the crown on beats 1 and 3
Alternating two-arm overhead pass with locked core
Half-tempo strike and freeze to develop control

lesson_ladder.goal: Connect arm rotations with rhythmic foot stepping at disco tempo (120 BPM)
drills: Continuous forward-and-back arm wrapping while stepping side-to-side
Double-time arm rotation into a 1-beat freeze pose
Directional level changes: drop to lunge while sustaining overhead rolls

lesson_ladder.goal: Express theatrical Hollywood drama through spontaneous cypher battles
drills: 3-pose character sequence interpreting an emotional song lyric
Continuous battle entry: 8-count travel, 8-count rapid whacks, dramatic exit freeze
Rhythmic syncopation challenge over unexpected disco breaks

visual_motifs: Spun disco balls reflecting fractured light across spinning forearms
Vintage black-and-white Hollywood movie stills intercut with modern club cyphers
Slow-motion captures of wrists wrapping around the crown of the head
episode_brief.instructor_persona: A sharp, charismatic street-dance historian and master waacker who insists on dramatic musical intention and historical respect.
episode_brief.music_cue: An uptempo 1970s disco track with surging strings, snapping hi-hats, and explosive brass stabs.

connections.name: Locking
connections.note: Developed in Los Angeles clubs during the same early 1970s era, sharing fast arm dynamics but created in funk club culture rather than queer disco spaces.

connections.name: Vogue
connections.note: Developed in parallel during the 1970s within queer ballroom communities on the East Coast of the United States.

seniors.seated_version: Perform arm circles, wrist rolls, and dramatic diva head-and-hand poses from a stable upright chair.
seniors.standing_version: Stationary standing practice focusing exclusively on shoulder mobility, arm framing, and upper-body poses without fast floor travel.
seniors.tempo_and_range: Reduce disco track speed to 80-90 BPM; keep arm sweeps below shoulder level if overhead mobility is restricted.
seniors.counts: 4-count slow arm wraps followed by 4-count holding poses.

children.game_version: Freeze Fame: kids perform continuous arm rolls to disco music and freeze instantly into movie superhero or star poses when the track stops.
children.counts: Even 8-count beats: 4 beats of arm winding, 4 beats of dramatic posing.

gaps: Specific named footwork patterns and step-by-step counts are sparsely detailed in the historical sources, which focus heavily on arm movements and posing.
Full original club discography tracklists are not enumerated in the encyclopedia texts beyond references to disco, funk, electro, and specific commercial tracks.

claims.text: Waacking originated from punking, a dance created in the gay clubs of Los Angeles during the 1970s disco era.
claims.quote: with origins stemming from punking, a dance created in the gay clubs of Los Angeles during the 1970s disco era.

claims.text: The movement was characterized by moving the arms rhythmically over the head.
claims.quote: The term "whack" was a specific movement within the punking style which involved moving the arms over the head in a rhythmic fashion.

claims.text: Jeffrey Daniel modified the name from waackin to waacking.
claims.quote: Later, dancer and singer-songwriter Jeffrey Daniel added the "g" to waackin to make it "waacking", the name by which the style is commonly known today.

claims.text: Dancers took stylistic inspiration from classic Hollywood screen stars.
claims.quote: Another big influence on waacking was Hollywood, whereby dancers took inspiration stylistically from movie stars such as Lauren Bacall, Marlene Dietrich, Bette Davis, and James Dean.

claims.text: The dance style was developed by the LGBTQ+ community, especially African American and Latino dancers.
claims.quote: Er ist ein Teil der Street-Dance-Kultur und wurde von der LGBTQ+-Community entwickelt, insbesondere von afroamerikanischen und lateinamerikanischen Tänzern.

claims.text: The AIDS crisis in the 1980s and 1990s killed most iconic dancers, leading waacking to almost disappear.
claims.quote: Dans les années 1980 et 1990, avec la crise du SIDA, la plupart des danseurs iconiques de l'époque meurent et le waacking disparaît presque.

claims.text: Brian Green began teaching waacking in 2003 to address the lack of transmission.
claims.quote: En 2003, Brian Green, dit « Footwork », dénonce le manque de transmission de cette culture et se met à enseigner la discipline, qui gagne rapidement en popularité
